# Sector Overview {#sec-sector-overview}

The chapters that follow describe how CIMS represents each part of the economy. Each sector is its own sub-model: a map of the products the sector makes, the steps that make them, and the energy those steps use. All the sectors are built from the same few ideas, which this chapter sets out once: a tree of steps linked by fixed amounts of input per unit of output, technologies that compete at the end of each branch, and a split between what a sector makes and the supporting services it uses. The chapter ends with a map of the sectors and the conventions they share.

## How a sector is modelled

CIMS represents a sector as a **flow model**: a chain of the activities needed to make the sector's output. The model tracks energy and technology, not money, and it is simpler than an engineer's process diagram. Each step in the chain is a place where CIMS can estimate energy use on its own. The steps are arranged as a tree. Fixed ratios link each step to the steps below it: how much of each input a step needs to make one unit of its output. Technologies compete only at the ends of the branches.

## How demand moves down the tree

The model code stores each sector as a tree of nodes. Each node passes the demand it receives down to the nodes below it in one of two ways:

- A **fixed-ratio** node splits its demand among the nodes below it in set proportions. These proportions capture the steps a process can't skip. Making a tonne of cement, for example, always takes a set amount of clinker.
- A **competition** node shares its demand among technologies that can each do the same job. Each technology has a capital cost, an operating cost, an amount of output, the energy and services it uses, and the years it is available and lasts. CIMS turns these into a lifecycle cost and gives each technology a share of new purchases based on that cost, using the choice rule described in @sec-technology-competition. A heterogeneity setting controls how strongly shares respond to differences in cost.

Fixed-ratio nodes give a sector its shape, and competition nodes decide which equipment and fuels serve each step. Policies such as a carbon price, a regulation, or a subsidy work by changing the outcome of those competitions.

## Product and Service sub-trees

Each sector tree splits at the top into two parts:

- The **Product** sub-tree is the production chain itself: the steps that turn raw inputs into what the sector sells, such as tonnes of steel, floor space, or kilometres travelled. A forecast of the sector's output or activity drives it, and its shape is specific to each sector.
- The **Service** sub-tree holds the supporting services that production steps use rather than provide for themselves, such as space heating and cooling, lighting, machine drive, steam, fuel blends, and carbon capture. Gathering these shared loads in one place means CIMS describes each piece of equipment once, and lets more efficient equipment or a switch of fuel serve the whole sector.

### Shared services

The industrial sectors use the same supporting services, with the same competing technologies. They follow the end uses of the U.S. Energy Information Administration's Manufacturing Energy Consumption Survey (MECS); for example, **machine drive** splits into pumps, fans and blowers, compressed air, materials handling, and materials processing. The General Services part describes each shared service once:

| Shared service | Chapter |
|:---------------|:--------|
| Machine drive | @sec-machine-drive |
| Steam (heat supply, including cogeneration) | @sec-industrial-heat |
| Cogeneration and on-site power | @sec-cogen |
| HVAC and lighting | @sec-hvac-lighting |
| Fuel blends | @sec-fuel-blends |
| CO~2~ capture, transport, and storage | @sec-ccus |

: Shared services and the chapters that describe them {#tbl-shared-services}

Not every sector uses every service, and each sector also has services of its own, such as cokemaking in iron and steel, chemical recovery in pulp and paper, and mine haulage in mining. The buildings and transportation sectors define their own services, described in their chapters.

## The sectors

The sectors fall into a few groups, following how energy and materials move through the economy.

Energy supply covers the industries that produce and convert the fuels everyone else uses: [Coal Mining](sector_coal-mining.qmd), [Natural Gas](sector_natural-gas.qmd), [Petroleum Crude](sector_petroleum-crude.qmd), and [Petroleum Refining](sector_petroleum-refining.qmd) for fossil fuels; [Electricity](sector_electricity.qmd); and the low-carbon fuels made in [Biofuels](sector_biofuels.qmd) (ethanol, biodiesel, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, renewable natural gas, and pellets) and [Hydrogen](sector_hydrogen.qmd). Every other sector uses the fuels and electricity these sectors supply, so their emissions carry through the whole model.

Industry covers the sectors that make materials: [Mining](sector_mining.qmd), [Industrial Minerals](sector_industrial-minerals.qmd) (including cement and lime), [Chemicals](sector_chemicals.qmd), [Pulp and Paper](sector_pulp-and-paper.qmd), [Metal Smelting](sector_metal-smelting.qmd), [Iron and Steel](sector_iron-and-steel.qmd), the catch-all [Light Industrial](sector_light-industrial.qmd), and [Construction](sector_construction.qmd). These sectors have the most detailed production chains and the largest process heat and process emissions, and they are where carbon capture and deep fuel switching matter most.

Buildings covers the [Residential](sector_residential.qmd) and [Commercial](sector_commercial.qmd) sectors: the heating, cooling, lighting, and appliances of the building stock.

Transportation covers moving people and goods, in [Transportation (Passenger)](sector_transportation-passenger.qmd) and [Transportation (Freight)](sector_transportation-freight.qmd). Each splits its vehicles by mode and by engine type.

Land, waste, and removals covers sectors whose emissions come mostly from something other than burning fuel, so their activity is often counted directly in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent: [Waste](sector_waste.qmd) (landfill methane), [Agriculture](sector_agriculture.qmd), and [Forestry](sector_forestry.qmd), along with [Direct Air Capture](sector_direct-air-capture.qmd), which removes CO₂ from the air, and [LULUCF](sector_lulucf.qmd) (land use, land-use change, and forestry). Several of these are simple placeholders today, and their chapters say what a fuller version would add.

## What each sector chapter contains

The sector chapters share one layout, so that each part of the economy answers the same questions:

- *Scope* says what the sector includes and leaves out, and where nearby activities are covered so nothing is counted twice.
- *Context* describes the real industry: its size in Canada, where its emissions come from, and the main ways to cut them.
- A *process flowchart* shows the steps that turn the sector's inputs into its products, the services those steps use, and the flows between them. The flowcharts show the sector's structure, not just how it runs today: they name purchased fuels only in general terms, because many newer technologies remove the need for a particular fuel. All the flowcharts share one visual style, described in @sec-figure-style.
- *Model structure* walks through the steps in the order of the flowchart. Each step is followed by a table of its technologies: the archetypes from the CIMS technology database that compete to provide it, each with a short description and its type (conventional, efficiency variant, alternative, or prospective). Shared services are listed by name, with a link to the General Services chapter that holds their technologies.
- *Decarbonisation* draws out the main ways those technologies can cut the sector's emissions.
- *Regional coverage* notes which regions carry the sector and how they differ, and *limitations and planned extensions* records known gaps and future work.

Where it helps, the chapters cite the sources the technology database draws on for a technology. The tables give only a summary; the technology database's archetype table holds the full set of values for every technology, including costs, energy use, lifetimes, emissions, and sources.

## Shared conventions

A few conventions apply to every sector chapter.

*One tree for all regions.* Each sector tree is written once and then set up for each of the seven modelled regions: Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan. The regions share the structure but differ in their activity forecasts, fuel prices, and how clean their electricity is. Not every sector appears in every region; coal mining, for instance, appears only where coal is mined.

*Behavioural discount rates.* Technology choices use discount rates drawn from how firms and households actually behave, not their financial cost of borrowing. These rates are higher, because they reflect short payback expectations and other barriers to investment. CIMS uses them throughout the lifecycle cost calculation, as set out in the [Theory](theory.qmd) chapter and in @sec-technology-competition.

*Emissions accounting.* Emissions include the CO₂ from the fuels each technology burns, process emissions released by chemical reactions rather than combustion (such as the CO₂ released when limestone is heated to make cement), and, in a few sectors, methane that leaks or is vented. All are counted as CO₂-equivalent, so gases with a stronger warming effect count at their full weight. Fuels reach the sectors as blends, so as the renewable share of a blend rises, every technology that burns it emits less. **Carbon capture** is a shared service that sectors can use where it applies.

These shared structures let CIMS treat a landfill, a steel mill, and a fleet of cars in one consistent way: each is a flow model of competing technologies, driven by a forecast of activity, using behavioural discount rates, and counted on a common emissions basis.
